background:
2 Timothy: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes

Study notes · dates are approximate and scholars vary

At a glance

2 Timothy is Paul's farewell. Imprisoned in Rome again, abandoned by many, and expecting execution, he writes to Timothy to pass on the gospel, endure hardship and come quickly. By tradition it is his last letter, about AD 66–67, under Nero.

QuestionTraditional viewNotes
AuthorPaul (1:1)One of the Pastoral Letters; many scholars question Paul's authorship, while the traditional view holds it is his. Its personal details are vivid.
DateAbout AD 66–67During a second Roman imprisonment, after Nero's persecution began in AD 64.
Written fromPrison in Rome (1:17)Unlike the earlier house arrest, Paul is in chains, hard to find, and expects death (1:16–17; 4:6).
RecipientTimothy, probably still in EphesusPaul's “beloved child” (1:2), whose faith came from his grandmother Lois and mother Eunice (1:5).
Situation“I am already being offered” (4:6)At his first hearing no one stood by him (4:16). Only Luke is with him (4:11).
RequestsCome before winter; bring Mark, my cloak and the books (4:9–13, 21)We do not know if Timothy arrived in time.

The letter's charge is to keep the gospel and pass it on: “the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2:2).

The time map

The shaded band marks about AD 66–67. The Great Fire and Nero's attack on Christians were recent memories, and the Jewish revolt had just begun.

Rome after the fire

Paul's second imprisonment came in the most dangerous years the church in Rome had yet faced.

  • The Great Fire (AD 64). Fire destroyed much of Rome. To end rumors that he had started it, Nero blamed the Christians.
  • Persecution. Tacitus writes that a “huge multitude” of Christians were arrested and killed, some torn by dogs, some crucified, some burned as torches at night.
  • Prison. Paul was no longer in a rented house but in chains, and friends had to search hard to find him (1:16–17). Later tradition links him to the Mamertine prison by the Forum.
  • Trial. At his “first defence” no one stood with him, yet the Lord strengthened him to preach (4:16–17).
  • Execution. Tradition says Paul, as a Roman citizen, was beheaded rather than crucified, on the road to Ostia outside Rome, about AD 67.
  • Nero's end. About a year later, in AD 68, Nero took his own life as the empire turned against him.

Facing death in Nero's Rome, Paul writes, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith” (4:7).

Paul's scattered friends

2 Timothy 4 gives a moving snapshot of Paul's team at the end.

  • Timothy. In Ephesus or nearby; Paul urges him to come before winter, when shipping stopped (4:21).
  • Luke. “Only Luke is with me” (4:11).
  • Mark. Once the young man who deserted Paul (Acts 15:38), now “useful to me for ministering” (4:11).
  • Demas. “Having loved this present world,” he left for Thessalonica (4:10).
  • Others. Crescens went to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia (on the Adriatic coast), Tychicus to Ephesus; Erastus stayed in Corinth; Trophimus was left sick at Miletus (4:10–20).
  • Onesiphorus. An Ephesian believer who searched Rome to find Paul and was not ashamed of his chains (1:16–18).
  • Alexander the coppersmith. “Did me much evil” (4:14); Timothy should beware of him.

Around the world in AD 66–67

Paul's last letter was written as the Roman world was entering turmoil.

RegionWhat was happening
BritainBoudica's revolt (AD 60–61). The queen of the Iceni burned London, Colchester and St Albans before being crushed.
RomeNero's early good years ended about AD 62. The Great Fire of AD 64 was followed by the first persecution of Christians.
JudeaTension grew; James the Lord's brother was killed in AD 62. The Jewish revolt broke out in AD 66.
Armenia and ParthiaA compromise peace in AD 63; Nero crowned the Parthian prince Tiridates king of Armenia in Rome in AD 66.
ItalyAn earthquake damaged Pompeii and Herculaneum in AD 62, seventeen years before Vesuvius buried them.
ChinaThe Eastern Han dynasty under Emperor Ming; silk reached Rome along the trade routes.
IndiaThe Kushan Empire was forming in the northwest; tradition says Thomas preached in India.
The AmericasTeotihuacan was growing; the Moche and Nazca cultures flourished in Peru.

How the setting shapes the study

2 Timothy's images and details fit Paul's last months in Nero's Rome.

PassageConnection to the times
2 Tim 1:8, 16After the fire, being linked to a chained Christian prisoner was dangerous.
2 Tim 2:3–4A soldier on active duty could not engage in civilian business.
2 Tim 2:5Athletes in the games had to compete by the rules to win the wreath.
2 Tim 2:20Great houses had vessels of gold and silver as well as wood and clay.
2 Tim 3:1–5Roman moralists also lamented the vices of their age.
2 Tim 4:6“Being offered” is the language of a drink offering poured out on an altar.
2 Tim 4:8Victors at the games received a crown; Paul expects “the crown of righteousness.”
2 Tim 4:13A heavy traveling cloak for a cold prison; books and parchments, perhaps Scripture.
2 Tim 4:21Sailing stopped in winter, so Timothy had to come before then.

Paul's last recorded words look beyond Nero's court: “The Lord will deliver me from every evil work, and will save me unto his heavenly kingdom” (4:18).

Maps: then and now

From prison in Rome Paul thinks of friends spread across the empire, from Dalmatia to Galatia, and asks Timothy to come from Asia before winter closed the sea lanes.

Today these places are in Italy, Greece, Croatia and Türkiye. A basilica in Rome, St. Paul Outside the Walls, stands over the traditional site of his tomb.

items.text: Greeting and Thanksgiving
Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, according to the promise of the life which is in Christ Jesus,
to Timothy, my beloved child: Grace, mercy, peace, from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
I thank God, whom I serve from my forefathers in a pure conscience, how unceasing is my remembrance of thee in my supplications, night and day
longing to see thee, remembering thy tears, that I may be filled with joy;
having been reminded of the unfeigned faith that is in thee; which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice; and, I am persuaded, in thee also.
For which cause I put thee in remembrance that thou stir up the gift of God, which is in thee through the laying on of my hands.
For God gave us not a spirit of fearfulness; but of power and love and discipline.
Not Ashamed of the Gospel
Be not ashamed therefore of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner: but suffer hardship with the gospel according to the power of God;
who saved us, and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before times eternal,
but hath now been manifested by the appearing of our Saviour Christ Jesus, who abolished death, and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel,
whereunto I was appointed a preacher, and an apostle, and a teacher.

For which cause I suffer also these things: yet I am not ashamed; for I know him whom I have believed, and I am persuaded that he is able to guard that which I have committed unto him against that day.
Hold the pattern of sound words which thou hast heard from me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
That good thing which was committed unto thee guard through the Holy Spirit which dwelleth in us.
This thou knowest, that all that are in Asia turned away from me; of whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes.
The Lord grant mercy unto the house of Onesiphorus: for he oft refreshed me, and was not ashamed of my chain;
but, when he was in Rome, he sought me diligently, and found me
(the Lord grant unto him to find mercy of the Lord in that day); and in how many things he ministered at Ephesus, thou knowest very well.

summary.title: CHAPTER 1 IN SUMMARY
paras: Paul, writing from prison, thanks God as he remembers Timothy night and day, longing to see him and recalling his tears. He remembers Timothy's sincere faith, which lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice, and urges him to rekindle the gift of God he received, “For God gave us not a spirit of fearfulness; but of power and love and discipline.”

Timothy must not be ashamed of the testimony of the Lord or of Paul His prisoner, but share in suffering for the gospel by the power of God, who saved us by grace, given in Christ Jesus, who “abolished death, and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel.” Paul is not ashamed, for he knows whom he has believed. He urges Timothy to hold to sound words and guard the good deposit. Everyone in Asia has turned away from him, but Onesiphorus searched him out in Rome and often refreshed him.

questions.label: OBSERVE
questions.text: What does Paul recall about Timothy's family faith in verse 5, and what does he urge Timothy to stir up and not be ashamed of (vv. 6–8)?

questions.label: THEN
questions.text: Why might believers in Asia have turned away from Paul (v. 15) when associating with a prisoner in Rome could bring shame and danger?

questions.label: NOW
questions.text: Onesiphorus sought Paul out and was not ashamed of his chain (vv. 16–18); whom could you seek out who feels isolated or forgotten?

items.text: A Good Soldier of Christ Jesus
Thou therefore, my child, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.
And the things which thou hast heard from me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
Suffer hardship with me, as a good soldier of Christ Jesus.
No soldier on service entangleth himself in the affairs of this life; that he may please him who enrolled him as a soldier.
And if also a man contend in the games, he is not crowned, except he have contended lawfully.
The husbandman that laboreth must be the first to partake of the fruits.
Consider what I say; for the Lord shall give thee understanding in all things.
Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, of the seed of David, according to my gospel:
wherein I suffer hardship unto bonds, as a malefactor; but the word of God is not bound.
Therefore I endure all things for the elect’s sake, that they also may obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory.
Faithful is the saying: For if we died with him, we shall also live with him:
if we endure, we shall also reign with him: if we shall deny him, he also will deny us:
if we are faithless, he abideth faithful; for he cannot deny himself.
A Worker Approved by God
Of these things put them in remembrance, charging them in the sight of the Lord, that they strive not about words, to no profit, to the subverting of them that hear.
Give diligence to present thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, handling aright the word of truth.
But shun profane babblings: for they will proceed further in ungodliness,
and their word will eat as doth a gangrene: of whom is Hymenæus and Philetus;
men who concerning the truth have erred, saying that the resurrection is past already, and overthrow the faith of some.
Howbeit the firm foundation of God standeth, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his: and, Let every one that nameth the name of the Lord depart from unrighteousness.
Now in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and of silver, but also of wood and of earth; and some unto honor, and some unto dishonor.
If a man therefore purge himself from these, he shall be a vessel unto honor, sanctified, meet for the master’s use, prepared unto every good work.
But flee youthful lusts, and follow after righteousness, faith, love, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart.
But foolish and ignorant questionings refuse, knowing that they gender strifes.
And the Lord’s servant must not strive, but be gentle towards all, apt to teach, forbearing,
in meekness correcting them that oppose themselves; if peradventure God may give them repentance unto the knowledge of the truth,
and they may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil, having been taken captive by him unto his will.

summary.title: CHAPTER 2 IN SUMMARY
paras: Timothy must be strong in grace and entrust what he has heard from Paul to faithful men who will teach others also. He must share in suffering as a good soldier of Christ Jesus, compete according to the rules like an athlete, and work hard like a farmer. “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, of the seed of David.” Paul suffers in chains, “but the word of God is not bound,” and he endures everything for the elect's sake.

Timothy should remind the church not to quarrel about words, and strive to be “a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, handling aright the word of truth.” He must avoid empty chatter like that of Hymenaeus and Philetus, who say the resurrection has already happened. In a great house there are honorable and dishonorable vessels; whoever cleanses himself will be useful to the Master. He must flee youthful lusts, pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace, and correct opponents with gentleness, in the hope that God will grant them repentance.

questions.label: OBSERVE
questions.text: What three images of soldier, athlete and farmer does Paul use in verses 3–6, and what does each teach about faithful ministry?

questions.label: THEN
questions.text: Why would the instruction to entrust teaching to faithful men who could teach others (v. 2) be crucial as the first generation of leaders began to die?

questions.label: NOW
questions.text: Paul urges gentleness in correcting opponents (vv. 24–26); how might you handle a present disagreement with patience rather than quarreling?

items.text: Godlessness in the Last Days
But know this, that in the last days grievous times shall come.
For men shall be lovers of self, lovers of money, boastful, haughty, railers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy,
without natural affection, implacable, slanderers, without self-control, fierce, no lovers of good,
traitors, headstrong, puffed up, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God;
holding a form of godliness, but having denied the power thereof: from these also turn away.
For of these are they that creep into houses, and take captive silly women laden with sins, led away by divers lusts,
ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth.
And even as Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses, so do these also withstand the truth; men corrupted in mind, reprobate concerning the faith.
But they shall proceed no further: for their folly shall be evident unto all men, as theirs also came to be.
All Scripture Is Inspired by God
But thou didst follow my teaching, conduct, purpose, faith, longsuffering, love, patience,
persecutions, sufferings; what things befell me at Antioch, at Iconium, at Lystra; what persecutions I endured: and out of them all the Lord delivered me.
Yea, and all that would live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.
But evil men and impostors shall wax worse and worse, deceiving and being deceived.
But abide thou in the things which thou hast learned and hast been assured of, knowing of whom thou hast learned them;
and that from a babe thou hast known the sacred writings which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
Every scripture inspired of God is also profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction which is in righteousness:
that the man of God may be complete, furnished completely unto every good work.

summary.title: CHAPTER 3 IN SUMMARY
paras: In the last days, Paul warns, people will be lovers of self and money, proud, abusive, disobedient, ungrateful, unholy, without love, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, having a form of godliness but denying its power. Timothy must turn away from such people, who creep into households, always learning but never coming to the truth, like the magicians who opposed Moses.

But Timothy has followed Paul's teaching, conduct, purpose, faith, patience, love and endurance, and seen the persecutions he suffered at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra, from which the Lord rescued him. All who desire to live godly in Christ Jesus will be persecuted. Timothy should continue in what he has learned, knowing from whom he learned it, and how from childhood he has known the sacred writings, which make him wise unto salvation through faith in Christ. “Every scripture inspired of God is also profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction which is in righteousness.”

questions.label: OBSERVE
questions.text: What traits of people in the last days are listed in verses 1–5, and how does Paul contrast Timothy's path in verses 10–11?

questions.label: THEN
questions.text: How would Timothy's upbringing in the sacred writings from childhood (v. 15) have equipped him in a mixed Jewish and Greek family and city?

questions.label: NOW
questions.text: Scripture is described as profitable for teaching, reproof, correction and instruction (v. 16); which of these do you most need from it right now?

items.text: Preach the Word; Paul's Farewell
I charge thee in the sight of God, and of Christ Jesus, who shall judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom:
preach the word; be urgent in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort, with all longsuffering and teaching.
For the time will come when they will not endure the sound doctrine; but, having itching ears, will heap to themselves teachers after their own lusts;
and will turn away their ears from the truth, and turn aside unto fables.
But be thou sober in all things, suffer hardship, do the work of an evangelist, fulfil thy ministry.
For I am already being offered, and the time of my departure is come.
I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith:

henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give to me at that day; and not to me only, but also to all them that have loved his appearing.
Personal Instructions
Give diligence to come shortly unto me:
for Demas forsook me, having loved this present world, and went to Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia.
Only Luke is with me. Take Mark, and bring him with thee; for he is useful to me for ministering.
But Tychicus I sent to Ephesus.
The cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus, bring when thou comest, and the books, especially the parchments.
Alexander the coppersmith did me much evil: the Lord will render to him according to his works:
of whom do thou also beware; for he greatly withstood our words.
At my first defence no one took my part, but all forsook me: may it not be laid to their account.
But the Lord stood by me, and strengthened me; that through me the message might be fully proclaimed, and that all the Gentiles might hear: and I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion.
The Lord will deliver me from every evil work, and will save me unto his heavenly kingdom: to whom be the glory for ever and ever. Amen.
Final Greetings
Salute Prisca and Aquila, and the house of Onesiphorus.
Erastus remained at Corinth: but Trophimus I left at Miletus sick.
Give diligence to come before winter. Eubulus saluteth thee, and Pudens, and Linus, and Claudia, and all the brethren.
The Lord be with thy spirit. Grace be with you.

summary.title: CHAPTER 4 IN SUMMARY
paras: Paul solemnly charges Timothy before God and Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead: “preach the word; be urgent in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort.” The time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching but gather teachers to suit their own desires. Timothy must stay sober, endure suffering, do the work of an evangelist and fulfill his ministry. As for Paul, “I am already being offered… I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith,” and the crown of righteousness awaits him and all who love the Lord's appearing. Paul asks Timothy to come soon, for Demas has deserted him, others have gone to other places, and only Luke is with him. He should bring Mark, the cloak Paul left at Troas, and the books, especially the parchments, and beware of Alexander the coppersmith. At Paul's first defense no one stood by him, but the Lord stood with him and strengthened him to proclaim the message, and he was rescued from the lion's mouth. “The Lord will deliver me from every evil work, and will save me unto his heavenly kingdom.” After final greetings, he urges Timothy to come before winter.

questions.label: THEN

questions.label: NOW

wrap.title: 2 Timothy In Summary
paras: 2 Timothy is Paul's last will and testament. Written from a Roman prison after Nero's persecution had begun, it is the letter of a man who knows his life is ending. Many have deserted him; only Luke is with him. Yet the letter is not bitter or afraid. Paul writes to strengthen his “beloved child” Timothy to carry on.

The central charge is to guard the gospel and pass it on. Timothy must hold to the pattern of sound words, guard the good deposit entrusted to him, and commit it to faithful people who will teach others also. Scripture, inspired by God, equips him for this work, and he must “preach the word” whether people want to hear it or not.

Paul also calls Timothy to courage in suffering. God has not given a spirit of fear but of power, love and self-discipline. Like a soldier, an athlete and a farmer, Timothy must endure hardship for the sake of a greater reward. All who want to live godly lives in Christ will be persecuted, but the word of God is not bound, even when its messengers are.

The letter's deepest note is hope. Christ Jesus has abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel. Paul can face execution saying, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith,” knowing a crown of righteousness awaits him. The Lord who stood by him at his trial will bring him safely into His heavenly kingdom.
The message in one line: faithful servants of Christ guard the gospel, pass it on to others and endure suffering without shame, because the Lord who saved them will keep them and bring them home.
